title: Rose Hammock Preserves Local Native Culture Through Art and Education
summary:
A Sonoma County teacher and artist, Rose Hammock educates the next generation through hands-on native studies, foraging classes and traditional artwork.

The post Rose Hammock Preserves Local Native Culture Through Art and Education appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Growing up in Santa Rosa, Rose Hammock learned mostly about Plains Indians in school. But at home, she loved listening to her family’s native Pomo stories.

“All of my teachers were elders,” she remembers. In her teens, she had a realization. “I’m that next person in line to teach what they were teaching. I don’t want to wait till I’m an elder to teach things. I want to do it now.”

Hammock, who is Pomo, Wailacki, and Maidu, and an enrolled member of the Round Valley Indian Tribes, teaches hands-on native studies at Sonoma Earth School in Forestville. She also leads foraging classes at Ya-Ka-Ama Indian Educational Center, raises awareness about the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Relatives movement, and volunteers with the Pomo Project, where her basketry is on display through Nov. 19 at its annual art show. Hammock, 30, is a cultural force of nature, always reminding people: “We’re still here. We’re not a thing of the past.”

This time of the year

As we go into the winter, this is when we have less dancing and less ceremony. This is kind of a restful period for us, when a lot of storytelling happens. This is when we’re harvesting and processing the last of our acorn, and basket sticks. This is also a time that we’re working on our regalia, the traditional clothes that we dance with. It’s just a reminder for us to rest and take care of ourselves and to take care of each other.

Teaching the next generation

Sonoma Earth School is a good opportunity to teach students about my culture, because they’re on Southern Pomo land. It’s understanding to respect the oak trees because they produce acorns and that’s food. Or understanding what plants are traditional, that are medicine or food or basket materials. Once they get to high school, they will have more respect and understanding of native culture and native people.

Looking to the future

A lot of knowledge is going to leave when our elders pass away. Things like learning dance and songs; learning about basket weaving; learning how to process traditional foods. If we don’t take the time now to ask questions and spend time with those elders, when they pass away we can’t ask them anymore. Just sharing and educating — that’s what is going to help our people stay alive.

California Native Creations Art Show

On exhibit through Nov. 19, 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Finley Center, 2060 W. College Ave., Santa Rosa

title: Francis Ford Coppola Winery’s Rustic Restaurant To Close for $2 Million Makeover
summary:
Rustic, the Italian restaurant at director Francis Ford Coppola's namesake winery in Geyserville, will close for renovations of the winery's hospitality spaces.

The post Francis Ford Coppola Winery’s Rustic Restaurant To Close for $2 Million Makeover appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
We’re sending a misty arrivederci to the rich chocolate mousse al Francis, memories of “a tavola” and Coppola Family Meatballs.

Rustic, the Italian restaurant at Francis Ford Coppola Winery in Geyserville, will close in December after 16 years as part of a $2 million renovation of the winery’s hospitality spaces.

Construction is expected to take 90 to 120 days, according to the winery’s owners, Delicato Family Wines, with a reopening anticipated in spring 2027. Details of the new dining experience have not yet been announced.

The closure will affect Rustic employees, though the winery has not disclosed how many jobs will be impacted.

Film director Francis Ford Coppola sold his namesake winery to Napa-based Delicato Family Wines in 2021. In July 2025, Delicato eliminated at least a dozen positions at Francis Ford Coppola Winery, with most of the cuts affecting the Geyserville restaurant, according to two employees who were among those laid off.

Rustic has been a dining destination for locals and tourists for years, with a menu inspired by Coppola’s favorite foods and Italian heritage. In the weeks before the temporary closure, the restaurant plans to mark its 16-year history with a special menu highlighting some of the filmmaker’s favorite dishes.

The renovation is part of a broader investment in the winery’s hospitality program. Plans include updates to the pool café, expanded private-event offerings and a refresh of its movie memorabilia collection.

The winery said the changes will build on Coppola’s original vision of creating a “wine wonderland” that brings together food, wine, cinema and hospitality.

The tasting room and other winery experiences will remain open during construction.

title: Healdsburg’s Michelin-Starred Troubadour Featured in Apple TV’s “Knife Edge”
summary:
Healdsburg's Troubadour Bread & Bistro stars in the season finale, following the couple behind the restaurant as they chase Michelin recognition.

The post Healdsburg’s Michelin-Starred Troubadour Featured in Apple TV’s “Knife Edge” appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Healdsburg’s Troubadour Bread & Bistro is getting some serious screen time in an Apple TV documentary series executive produced by celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay.

That may be surprising for a neighborhood sandwich shop. But Troubadour has a second identity: At night, it transforms into an intimate fine-dining restaurant. And that’s only part of the story.

The eight-episode series, “Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars,” follows 16 restaurants around the world as their chefs pursue one of the culinary world’s most coveted distinctions: a Michelin star.

Troubadour appears in the season finale, “We Don’t Compromise,” released Nov. 5, alongside San Francisco’s Restaurant Naides, where chef Patrick Gabon and his partner, Celine Wuu, are working to bring Filipino cuisine into the Michelin spotlight.

Spoiler alert: Troubadour gets the star. I wrote about the restaurant’s win last July, so the outcome is hardly breaking news.

But the story behind it is just as compelling as it was during the anxious months leading up to Michelin’s announcement.

Chef Sean McGaughey and his wife, Melissa Yanc McGaughey, are best known for Quail & Condor, their award-winning Healdsburg bakery. But Sean’s more personal project, an ambitious French bistro with an elaborate tasting menu, earned Troubadour its first Michelin star in 2026.

A former punk-rock drummer who became a fine-dining chef before opening the bakery, McGaughey is not your typical tweezer-wielding culinary obsessive. He cooks on induction burners, serves dishes on thrifted Limoges china and lets Ludacris, Journey and Run-DMC provide the soundtrack.

This is not your average Michelin-starred restaurant.

Even knowing how the story ends, the documentary is a nail-biter. The cameras capture the couple’s anxiety over the bistro’s financial future as they open a new Healdsburg bakery and try to balance the demands of the business with family life.

It’s good television, made even better when you know the people involved.

Hosted by food and travel personality Jesse Burgess, the series goes behind the scenes at restaurants from California to Scandinavia, following chefs through the pressure, uncertainty and sometimes obsessive attention to detail that come with chasing Michelin recognition.

The second season of “Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars” is now streaming on Apple TV. The series has also been renewed for a third season.

title: Sonoma Author Megumi Inouye Uses Origami To Elevate the Art of Giving
summary:
Using an age-old Japanese art form, along with foraged and repurposed materials, Megumi Inouye brings thoughtfulness to the presentation of gifts.

The post Sonoma Author Megumi Inouye Uses Origami To Elevate the Art of Giving appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When Megumi Inouye gives a gift, her wrapping is so thoughtful and beautiful that the recipient may be reluctant to open it.

On walks near her home in Sonoma, she might pick up fall leaves or a cluster of milkweed to garnish a present. Last year’s calendar from El Molino restaurant might turn into a one-of-a-kind box or wrapping-paper collage. A foraged twig, woven through hole-punches in the paper, becomes the tie that binds.

In her new book “Origami Gift Wrap,” Inouye shares 25 tape-free techniques for decorating presents. It might seem complicated, but most of the step-by-step creations involve simple folding and measuring — and a dose of patience.

An origami heart or fanned pleats atop a present may seem curated for social media sharing, but there’s more beneath the veneer, just as wrapping a gift is more than just concealing what lies inside.

“Pared down to its essence, wrapping is simply a covering,” Inouye writes in the book, an updated paperback version of her previous book, “The Soul of Gift Wrapping.” “It is through our hands and our hearts, following the deepest of our instincts, that we make it into something of value.”

The magic of the book lies in her storytelling, unfolding in chapters of her life. At a young age, Inouye was mesmerized by the way her mother wrapped kimonos before storing them in drawers. It left an impression, one she carries today. Her wistful description of the last present she ever wrapped for her father is a gift to the reader. After retirement, he spent much of his time writing senryu, a Japanese form of short poetry based on daily observations. His work was often published in Japanese-American newspapers. She used newspaper, the only material she had on hand at the time, to wrap wooden blocks collaged with his poetry clippings.

“I feel like the book for me was this way to be holistic about wrapping. Not just looking at wrapping techniques, but thinking about why do we wrap? And why it’s meaningful,” says Inouye, who won a national gift-wrapping competition in 2009, later appearing on “The Ellen DeGeneres Show” to showcase her skills.

Inouye loves teaching readers to wrap in a way that she describes as “both nurturing to ourselves and other people, and also nurturing to our environment.” That includes repurposing and reusing materials to create new life from things we throw away, such as wrinkled tissue paper that’s often stuffed into gift bags and boxes. She reshapes it to create an ornate flower that is delightfully wabi-sabi, adhering to the Japanese notion of appreciating imperfection.

“The beauty of the presentation, thoughtfulness of the materials, and the loving intentions passed along in the act of wrapping are all gifts of care perhaps equal to the gift itself,” Inouye writes, adding new meaning to the expression “It’s the thought that counts” by wrapping it in an age-old Japanese art form.

Holiday Workshop

Learn the art of Origami Gift Wrapping with Megumi Inouye.

6-9 p.m. Nov. 17, Sonoma Community Center. sonomacommunitycenter.org

Learn more at giftwrapbymegumi.com.

title: SingleThread Cookbook Offers Rare Look Inside Healdsburg’s Three-Michelin-Starred Restaurant
summary:
The new book from Kyle and Katina Connaughton offers a behind-the-scenes look at the food, farming and philosophy behind Healdsburg's three-Michelin-starred restaurant.

The post SingleThread Cookbook Offers Rare Look Inside Healdsburg’s Three-Michelin-Starred Restaurant appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Raise your hand if you have a home food laboratory stocked with glutamic acid, liquid nitrogen and Ultra-Tex 3, a modified tapioca starch — and the time and equipment to make elderflower, hyssop and verjus foam or sea bean Dippin’ Dots.

Me neither. But it’s nice to know you could, if you really wanted to.

Two people who can are Kyle and Katina Connaughton, thanks to the elaborate setup at their three-Michelin-starred SingleThread restaurant in Healdsburg. Their new cookbook, “SingleThread: A Seasonal Approach to Intentional Cooking, Farming and Hospitality” ($75, DK), co-written with Georgia Freedman, offers an unusually intimate look at what it takes to run one of the world’s most celebrated restaurants.

Unless you have your own food lab at home, you probably won’t be making most of the recipes for dinner. But that’s not really the point of this nearly 400-page coffee-table book. Instead, it tells the story of the people, land, ingredients and labor behind the Connaughtons’ restaurant, farm and inn, following their work through the seasons.

It’s also a chance to go behind the scenes of a restaurant few diners will experience and the thinking behind each ingredient, dish and painstaking presentation.

“At SingleThread, the ‘why’ is at the heart of everything we do,” Kyle Connaughton said. “This book is our way of sharing that philosophy, and the stories behind them, so that readers can bring that same intention into their own kitchens and homes.”

At 7 pounds, the book could double as part of a daily workout: lift, read, lift, read.

A year at SingleThread

Organized around the four seasons, the book follows the rhythms of the farm and kitchen, showing how the two work together to create SingleThread’s elaborate multicourse tasting menus.

The Connaughtons’ approach draws on years spent living and working in Japan and later in England before returning to California to open SingleThread in 2016.

The restaurant quickly became a destination, earning three Michelin stars in 2018, a distinction it continues to hold. Today, it is one of only seven three-Michelin-starred restaurants in the Bay Area. It also recently ranked No. 93 on the extended 51-100 list of The World’s 50 Best Restaurants for 2026, making it the only U.S. restaurant on that portion of the list.

But this book is no victory lap through a decade of culinary accolades.

Inspired by Japanese culinary traditions, the Connaughtons embrace “shun,” the appreciation of ingredients at their seasonal peak, and “kaiseki,” a carefully considered progression of dishes that reflects the season.

Katina’s work on the farm and Kyle’s in the kitchen are closely intertwined. What grows on the farm shapes what the kitchen creates, while the dining room brings those ingredients to life through food, flowers, ceramics and a carefully choreographed 10-course menu.

Filled with lush photography, the book captures some of the more intangible aspects of SingleThread’s philosophy. Annotated photographs and intimate portraits help bring Japanese concepts such as “ikebana” (flower arranging), “omotenashi” (hospitality), “ichi-go ichi-e” (the fleeting nature of each moment) and “kaizen” (continuous improvement) to life in ways words alone can’t quite convey.

Hello and goodbye

SingleThread’s first course may be its most awe-inspiring and recognizable. Called a “hassun,” it’s a snapshot of the season, presented in a collection of small bites.

The sculptural arrangement of tiny dishes, nestled among flowers, moss and greenery gathered by Katina’s team, is breathtaking in its complexity. It can contain as many as 10 individual bites, and the display is constantly changing as shifts in climate bring new ingredients from the farm — and signal the departure of others.

The final produce of a season, available in limited quantities and at its peak, gets a last moment in the spotlight. It might be a late-ripening fall tomato or a late-winter carrot. Hence the idea and name behind the course: hello to the guests, goodbye to ingredients that won’t appear again until the following year.

The book documents these fleeting displays month by month. In early winter, there might be a honey mussel with clarified mussel dashi, chile oil and a tie of carrot and celtuce. In spring, wagyu beef tataki arrives with wasabina puree, grilled hakurei turnip, kinome and wasabi.

And whether or not you know what “kinome” is — a pepper tree leaf with a bright, tingling citrus flavor — the point is that it’s there for a reason, at precisely that moment in the season.

At the restaurant, these elaborate arrangements last only minutes before they’re dismantled and eaten. In the book, readers can linger over every detail, with ingredients identified and explained for food enthusiasts, like me, to further investigate.

Recipes for the rest of us

For home cooks, one of the most intriguing decisions the Connaughtons made was what to leave out.

Rather than trying to translate every elaborate SingleThread dish into something a reader could prepare on a Tuesday night, the book explains the more complicated techniques while offering foundational recipes and dishes that are somewhat more approachable.

Many of those recipes come from the inn, including donabe hot pots filled with seafood and vegetables, grilled salmon and Japanese omelets.

To be clear, these are not 30-minute sheet pan dinners with five ingredients. Making the omelet, for instance, requires a well-seasoned carbon-steel tamago pan, homemade dashi, white tamari and clarified butter. Ambitious, for sure, but not impossible.

The book also includes recipes for dashi, the delicate Japanese broth that forms the backbone of countless dishes, as well as ponzu, pickles, ferments and other staples of the SingleThread kitchen.

Will you make them all? Probably not. But unlike cookbooks that leave ambitious home cooks with a long shopping list, a sink full of dishes and the nagging suspicion that dinner would have been easier if they’d just made pasta, this one doesn’t seem particularly interested in making readers feel like a failure.

The real takeaway is a better understanding of why certain ingredients, preparations and techniques work together. It’s about paying attention to what’s in season and learning how even simple preparations can bring out the best in good ingredients.

The art of paying attention

Food is only part of the SingleThread experience. Just as much thought goes into how guests are treated.

The Japanese philosophy of “omotenashi,” often described as wholehearted hospitality, has been central to SingleThread since its beginning. Rather than waiting for guests to ask for something, the goal is to anticipate their needs and create an experience in which every detail feels effortless.

At the restaurant, that might mean the precise arrangement of flowers, the selection of a handmade ceramic dish or the progression of a meal that unfolds over several hours.

Sometimes, it translates into details guests may never notice: the DNA sequence of an onion woven into one of 12 handmade screens, each featuring the genetic sequence of a seasonal ingredient, or the precise width to which cucumbers must be cut because anything thicker or thinner changes their mouthfeel.

These subtle details are among the book’s greatest pleasures.

Freedman said working on the project revealed just how deliberately the Connaughtons approach every aspect of SingleThread.

“Nothing at SingleThread is accidental; the way a plate is composed, the flowers on the table, the order of a meal, the choice of what to grow each season, every detail has a carefully considered reason behind it,” she said.

Her hope, she added, is that readers will come away feeling as though they’ve spent a year on the farm and at the table.

Ten years, one big idea

The book’s publication marks a milestone for the Connaughtons, who have spent the past decade building a restaurant and agricultural operation that’s become one of Sonoma County’s most impressive culinary success stories.

This year, they also opened a new restaurant in Kyoto, Japan, and are preparing to debut the The Selvedge, a boutique hotel in Healdsburg. It’s been a busy year, but the journey has been far from effortless.

From high school sweethearts who met at a Southern California punk show to young parents making do in a remote Japanese town with leftover vegetables from Kyle’s restaurant job, their story is not exactly one of glamour or overnight success.

Months of work without a vacation, distance from friends and family, and the challenge of building a restaurant from scratch were only part of it. Floods, wildfires and a pandemic complicated SingleThread’s early years, too.

For Kyle, the book is a way to share what they have learned while creating something readers can return to.

“We wanted it to be something tangible, with stories, recipes, and inspiration readers want to spend time with and return to season after season,” he said.

For diners who have experienced SingleThread, the book offers a chance to revisit the food and better understand the work behind it. For those who haven’t, it’s a considerably less expensive way to explore the restaurant’s world without having to secure one of Sonoma County’s most coveted reservations.

The average home cook may never have access to SingleThread’s ingredients, equipment or team of talented cooks. But some of the underlying lessons are surprisingly accessible: Pay attention to what’s in season. Buy good ingredients. Waste less. Take care with the details.

You don’t need three Michelin stars — or a tamago pan — to do any of that.

For more on the couple behind SingleThread, including their family life, holiday traditions and what drives them, read Heather Irwin’s profile of Kyle and Katina Connaughton in the November/December issue of Sonoma Magazine.

title: The Gentle Hearth Is on a Mission To Save the Gravenstein, One Pie at a Time
summary:
As Sonoma County's apple industry faces mounting challenges, The Gentle Hearth steps in to help preserve the Gravenstein with seasonal pies and year-round pantry products.

The post The Gentle Hearth Is on a Mission To Save the Gravenstein, One Pie at a Time appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Cameron Woodruff is a problem solver, and he’s doing it with pie. A piano technician who rebuilds Steinway concert grand pianos, Woodruff has taken on a second identity as a baker and entrepreneur, compelled by what he saw as a need for something — anything — to help the local apple industry at a critical moment, particularly the celebrated Gravenstein apple.

“Everyone has this sentiment of not wanting to see them disappear,” he says of the heirloom variety. “The most fundamental aspect is demand.” So Woodruff set out to create it. A year ago, the 42-year-old Forestville resident launched The Gentle Hearth and began selling pies, mustard, and barbecue sauce made with Gravenstein apples at the beginning of 2026.

He works out of commercial kitchens in Sebastopol, including one on a rural property south of town. The drive takes you past Apple Blossom Elementary School, Appleseed Lane, and barns and houses adorned with botanical imagery, leaving little doubt you’re in apple country — or at least what remains of it.

One Friday afternoon, the aroma of freshly baked pastry and cinnamon drifted through the autumn air, an olfactory compass pointing the way toward Woodruff and his small kitchen crew as they peeled and sliced Gravenstein apples for 24 pies he would take to the farmers markets over the weekend.

It was a modest, manageable batch compared with the 300 pies he baked for the 2026 Gravenstein Apple Fair, an undertaking that pushed the small commercial kitchens where he works to their limits. But if anyone can find a way to make the most of the limited capacity, it’s Woodruff.

The pie recipe belonged to his grandmother. Growing up in Marin County, Woodruff often spent idyllic weekends visiting his grandparents, Gene and Marilyn Malm, in Occidental. Their home had a small orchard, and Marilyn’s Gravenstein pies were the highlight of family gatherings. When Woodruff created The Gentle Hearth, he drew on those memories. “I wanted to do something to capture these feelings I was fortunate enough to have on my grandparents’ property and to bring that joy to others,” he says.

One of the first people to recognize the promise of his pies was Peter Bettendorff, a baker who makes a wildly popular gluten-free almond cake sold at Sebastopol Cookie Company. Bettendorff has since become a member of his kitchen crew.

The first time Bettendorff tried one of Woodruff’s pies, the two were standing at the tailgate of Woodruff’s truck outside Safeway. One bite, he says, and he was sold. “It was an epiphany in a parking lot.”

The distinguishing feature of Woodruff’s pies is their olive oil crust. The filling is comparatively straightforward: sugar, cinnamon, a few spices he declines to disclose, and local apples — naturally. “The recipe is secondary,” explains Woodruff. “If the apples are delicious, you’re going to have a great pie.”

Sonoma County apples are largely dry-farmed, a practice that produces crisp, firm, and intensely flavorful fruit. Supermarket apples shipped in from elsewhere are no substitute. FEED Cooperative, a local food hub that works with dozens of farms, says the average grocery store apple is 14 months old, with flavor and nutritional value diminishing with each passing day.

That dependence on local fruit means Woodruff’s pie season has an expiration date. He freezes some apples to extend production, but when that supply runs out, he won’t turn to grocery store apples to keep the ovens going. Instead, he uses Gravensteins in pantry products: a barbecue sauce made with smoked apple syrup, applesauce and apple cider vinegar, and a mustard made with apple syrup, apple cider vinegar, and avocado oil infused with frozen peels left over from pie making. The peels lend another layer of apple flavor while helping to reduce waste. Woodruff is developing other products, too, including sauerkraut made with cabbage and apple peels.

A student working toward a civil engineering degree at Santa Rosa Junior College, Woodruff is constantly refining recipes and processes, looking for ways to improve quality and efficiency. Before investing in a pie press he found in Canada, he built a prototype. To speed up the tedious task of dotting pie filling with cubes of butter, he found another solution: a three-holed sauce dispenser that squirts softened butter over the filling before adding the top crust.

These are relatively small, solvable problems. The challenges facing the local apple industry are considerably larger.

Orchard acreage has dwindled to about 2,000 acres in 2024, down from 14,000 during the Gravenstein’s heyday. Now the county faces the impending departure of Manzana Products Co., its last remaining processing plant, which is scheduled to end operations and move to Washington by next year.

Woodruff is under no illusion that one pie business can reverse decades of decline. But he believes it can help. “You’ve got to start somewhere,” he says. “I can do my part and I hopefully will inspire others. Within a year, I’m making really good headway.”

His ambitions extend beyond his current operation. In the coming year, he hopes to work out of a new apple processing plant in Santa Rosa purchased earlier this year by Brooke Hazen, the owner of Gold Ridge Organic Farms in Sebastopol. Woodruff says the facility has a walk-in oven capable of baking 240 pies at a time — an exponential leap from where he’s at now. Still, even thousands of pies may not be enough to restore the industry.

Carole Flaherty, a member of Slow Food Russian River and coordinator of the Save Our Orchards project, has spent years confronting the problem. At 80, she continues to tend 200 apple trees of her own. One priority, she says, is persuading more grocery stores to stock local apples, either instead of or alongside fruit trucked in from Washington or elsewhere. Another is finding people willing to maintain the orchards, particularly the backyard plots that have long been part of the region’s agricultural landscape. “These guys are aging out, and we don’t see anybody in the wings to take it on,” says Flaherty.

Her concern is unmistakable. But the efforts of Woodruff and others, including Gold Ridge Organic Farms, Little Apple Treats, and local cideries, offer reason for optimism.

For Woodruff, the immediate challenge is Thanksgiving. He needs to establish a system for taking holiday orders and determine where customers can pick up their pies. Beyond that lies a more complicated question: the Gravenstein apple cider vinegar and applesauce he uses in his products are made by Manzana. When the company leaves for Washington, his local source for those ingredients disappears with it. But that’s a problem for another day. “I’ll figure it out as I go,” he says.

For now, Woodruff is content to play a small part in addressing a problem with no easy answers. Every pie he sells creates another reason to grow, harvest, and preserve the Gravenstein. In an industry struggling to find its footing, that counts for something.

Find The Gentle Hearth

Saturdays from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Santa Rosa Original Certified Farmers Market, 50 Mark West Springs Road, Santa Rosa. Order pies online at thegentlehearth.com.

title: Goguette Bread Opens Hidden Wine Bar in Santa Rosa
summary:
Bistroquette de Goguette is a tiny hideaway with about 20 seats, inspired by childhood memories, good bread and the pleasure of doing absolutely nothing.

The post Goguette Bread Opens Hidden Wine Bar in Santa Rosa appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Open the door to Bistroquette de Goguette, and you step through a magic portal into a neighborhood wine bar in Paris. Not just any wine bar, but the place where owner Najine Shariat spent countless unhurried evenings with her family, sometimes falling asleep on a bench with her three sisters while their parents sipped wine and nibbled on bread and cheese.

It wasn’t a restaurant or a bar, really, but a third space where families could linger over a simple meal without spending much money or watching the clock. It wasn’t about the wine or the food; it was about the moment.

“My parents used to sit in a corner and grab a glass of wine, and no one would bother them. They could sit for three hours,” said Shariat.

Something almost unheard of in the United States: Who has three hours to drink wine and eat bread?

That’s precisely why Shariat has brought this cherished childhood memory to life, right down to the black-and-white mosaic floor tiles, wrought-iron bistro tables, long banquettes and dim lighting. Even the wall color, a hard-to-pin-down shade somewhere between dark forest green and midnight blue, is the same. Or at least pretty close, she said.

Now Shariat hopes to give her Sonoma County neighbors a little of what she remembers: a place to gather over a glass of wine and a basket of bread with salted butter.

A place to slow down, put away the phones and stay awhile.

Part speakeasy, part wine bar

The small wine bar adjoining Goguette Bread in Santa Rosa has no sign, no sandwich board with daily specials outside and no obvious indication that it’s even there. It’s intentionally hidden in plain sight, known mostly to Goguette regulars and through word of mouth. Reservations are recommended, though customers can check in at the bakery to see if there’s space.

“If you know, you know,” she said with a grin.

The secrecy isn’t about exclusion, but about keeping the space intimate, without pressure to turn tables quickly.

Shariat, who co-owns the Parisian bakery with her husband, Nas Salamati, said the adjoining space was originally intended for a larger production kitchen. At least, that’s what Salamati wanted. She had something very different in mind.

“I really wanted this for me,” she admitted. Salamati acquiesced.

The usually bubbly Shariat, dressed in a black-and-white striped shirt and white baker’s cap, pauses when the conversation turns to her mother, who died in May. Her eyes well up as she explains why opening the wine bar suddenly became so important.

“I had to do something,” she said of her decision in August to create Bistroquette.

What began as an idea for a neighborhood gathering spot, and a way to add seating to the busy bakery, became a tribute to her parents and the evenings they spent together in Paris.

Pointing around the room, she tells the story of each piece of furniture and art: mismatched antique mirrors from Southern California that she strapped to the roof of her car, impossibly heavy bistro tables from France, upholstered wooden church pews donated and installed by members of a Portuguese church, and her sister’s original artwork on the walls.

Bistroquette de Goguette is truly a labor of love. Emphasis on the labor. But also the love.

The menu

This is Goguette, of course, so bread always has a starring role.

The short Bistroquette menu includes a basket of assorted breads with French salted butter, charcuterie, baguette sandwiches — ham and cheese or ham and butter — and a green olive and roasted sweet pepper fougasse made especially for the wine bar.

“The idea is to keep it simple, not overwhelm people,” she said.

There’s also the bakery’s luscious custard-style ice cream — the chocolate-orange is outstanding — available by the cup or as an affogato with espresso. Apple juice is available for children, who are welcome at the wine bar.

Bistroquette’s wine list is equally straightforward, with six or seven French and Sonoma County wines chosen for their easy drinkability, mostly $10 to $14 a glass. The selection includes Champagne and other sparkling wines, fruity red Gamay served chilled, rosé and a couple of whites, usually a Chardonnay from Burgundy and a local Sauvignon Blanc.

Orders are placed through a small window looking into the bakery, keeping the setup casual. Shariat and Salamati stop by to visit with customers and friends but spend most of their time in the bakery, leaving guests to enjoy themselves at their own pace.

“This is just a place to be and in the moment, to be transported somewhere else,” Shariat said, “and then walk out and go on with your life.”

Bistroquette de Goguette: Adjoining Goguette Bread, 59 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa, goguettebread.com. Open 1:30-9 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday. Closed Sunday through Tuesday. Enter through the bakery and ask about seating. Reservations recommended by emailing info@goguettebread.com.

title: Sonoma Botanical Garden Offers Unique Autumn Leaf-Peeping Experience
summary:
Boasting over 50 species of wild-origin Asian maples, this public botanical garden in Glen Ellen is an ideal spot for viewing autumn-leaf hues.

The post Sonoma Botanical Garden Offers Unique Autumn Leaf-Peeping Experience appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The maple collection at Sonoma Botanical Garden in Glen Ellen offers visitors a unique and rare glimpse of autumn hues, making it an ideal spot for leaf-peeping on a sunny, crisp fall day.

The garden, founded almost 40 years ago, boasts more than 50 species of wild-origin Asian maples. As autumn’s shorter days and cooler nights unlock the maples’ gold, crimson, and even purple hues, November is an ideal time to engage in the Japanese tradition of momijigari — or autumn-leaf hunting.

The garden has several guided events through November, including a Fall Color Walk Nov. 20-22, but the park is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily so visitors can explore the spectacle at their own pace.

The five-lobed maple (Acer pentaphyllum) is one of the last species to flaunt its crimson foliage, often extending the season into early December. While traveling to and from the garden along Highway 12, Sonoma Valley vineyards put on their own vibrant display, ensuring a flamboyant and fabulous fall outing.

12841 Highway 12, Glen Ellen. 707-996-3166, sonomabg.org

title: Mozaik Restaurant in Sonoma Gets Surprise Visit From Tyra Banks
summary:
“America’s Next Top Model” creator Tyra Banks surprised a local restaurant on the Sonoma Plaza with a recent visit.

The post Mozaik Restaurant in Sonoma Gets Surprise Visit From Tyra Banks appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Supermodel, actress and producer Tyra Banks traded the catwalk for a Sonoma stroll this week when she made a surprise visit to a Sonoma Plaza restaurant. The “America’s Next Top Model” creator and judge dined at Mozaik, the global cuisine-focused restaurant that replaced Sonoma’s Sausage Emporium in 2024.

Mozaik owner Miranda Ives, who founded Sausage Emporium in 2021 before expanding to gyros, poke bowls, umami burgers and Kashmiri tacos, took a selfie with Banks and posted it on Instagram after her visit.

“It was a lovely surprise in the middle of an already buzzing Friday evening,” the social media post stated regarding Banks’ visit.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by MOZAIK (@mozaik_sonoma)

The post also said Banks ordered the restaurant’s signature mashed potatoes and sticky ribs, while the rest of her party enjoyed Kashmiri tacos, Sichuan wontons and Thai green curry chicken.

Mozaik draws on Ives’ world travels, serving a diverse menu in a prime Plaza location. Last year, the restaurant added more outdoor seating and an accessible ramp.

In addition to “America’s Next Top Model,” Banks is known for her stint as a Victoria’s Secret Angel, hosting her own talk show, “The Tyra Banks Show,” and co-staring in Disney’s 2000 fantasy comedy “Life-Size” alongside Lindsay Lohan. Her talk show won a Daytime Emmy Award in 2008 and 2009. Banks was also the first Black woman featured on the covers of GQ magazine and the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue.

This wasn’t Banks’ first foray into Wine Country — in 2016, Banks and her mother went through an “intensive boot camp” experience at the Culinary Institute of America in Napa.

Banks’ visit to Mozaik is one of many celebrity sightings in Sonoma County, where the stars come to dine on world-class cuisine and even launch their own wine brands.

“Thank you, Tyra, for choosing Mozaik,” the restaurant’s Instagram post stated. “It was an absolute pleasure having you with us!”

Mozaik is located at 31 E. Napa St., Sonoma. 707-934-8814, mozaiksonoma.com

title: Alter Egos: Traditional Local Wine Brands Show Their Adventurous Side
summary:
Local winemakers are taking a chance on experimenting with wine. Here are three “dual-personality” brands in Wine Country worth discovering.

The post Alter Egos: Traditional Local Wine Brands Show Their Adventurous Side appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Newer wineries with a natural bent aren’t the only ones fermenting outside the box. Long-established producers are also branching out, and some have even launched adventurous side brands. The idea is to give winemakers a chance to have fun and experiment while offering consumers — especially younger ones — a variety of wine styles to explore.

Here are three “dual-personality” wineries worth discovering.

Kokomo Winery/Breaking Bread

Winemaker Erik Miller founded his Healdsburg winery in 2004 and built a reputation for producing terrific Dry Creek Zinfandel, Alexander Valley Cabernet Sauvignon and a delicious rosé. Then, in 2018, he introduced Breaking Bread. Made in a lighter, lower-alcohol style than the Kokomo offerings, the lineup includes Zinfandel-based pet-nat and rosé, along with an orange wine, a whole cluster Pinot Noir, and Al Dente, a chillable Mourvèdre blend. Taste them at the Kokomo tasting room in Healdsburg. 4791 Dry Creek Road, Healdsburg, kokomowines.com; breakingbreadwines.com

Stewart Cellars/Guthrie Family Wines

When he’s not making serious, terroir-driven wines for Yountville-based Stewart Cellars — founded in 2000 by his father-in-law Michael Stewart — Blair Guthrie makes his own brand of wines at Guthrie Family Cellars in Sonoma. Guthrie takes a minimalist approach, starting with organically and biodynamically farmed grapes. Flavor profiles are bright and fresh, shining a spotlight on varieties such as Vermentino, Grenache Blanc and Gamay Noir. 6752 Washington St., Yountville, stewartcellars.com; guthriefamilywines.com

Obsidian Ridge/Rabbit Hole

Brothers Arpad and Peter Molnar launched Obsidian Ridge, their Lake County-based Cabernet Sauvignon brand, in 2002. Then, in 2020, they went down a rabbit hole. The Rabbit Hole line is a little on the wild side, taking an experimental, natural-leaning path. Current releases include a sparkling Pinot Noir pet-nat called Pezsgő, the Máslás red piquette and a sweet white vermouth. Taste the wines at Obsidian Ridge Base Camp in downtown Sonoma. 441 First St. W., Sonoma, obsidianwineco.com

This story was excerpted from our feature on Sonoma County Wineries Building a Brighter Future, originally published in the September/October 2026 issue of Sonoma Magazine.
